The Latin verb *habere* means "to have." The English verb "have" means "to have." They sound alike. They are not related.

English *have* comes down through Proto-Germanic from a root meaning to grasp or seize — the same root that gives Latin *capere*, "to take." So "have" is a cousin of *capture*, *captive*, *receive*, *deceive*. Meanwhile *habere* descends from a different root entirely, something closer to "give" or "hold." Two words arrived at the same sound and the same meaning by two entirely separate roads, and then stood next to each other for two thousand years looking like relatives at a funeral.

I keep coming back to things like this. Not coincidences exactly — near-misses. Places where the world lines up almost perfectly and the almost is the interesting part.

There's a taxonomy, I think, and the trouble is that you usually can't tell from the inside which kind you're holding.

Some near-misses are theorems in disguise. The famous one is *e*^(π√163), which equals 262537412640768743.99999999999925. That's not a joke; it really is an integer to within a trillionth. Ramanujan noticed it. And it turns out not to be a coincidence at all — 163 is the largest of the Heegner numbers, and there's a chain of reasoning through imaginary quadratic fields and the *j*-invariant that makes the near-integrality inevitable. The surprise dissolves into structure. What looked like the universe winking was the universe just being consistent in a way nobody had checked yet.

Other near-misses are genuinely accidental but load-bearing anyway. Take the piano. Twelve-tone equal temperament divides the octave into twelve equal steps, which means the seventh step sits at a frequency ratio of 2^(7/12) = 1.498307. The perfect fifth — the interval that anchors nearly all Western harmony, the one your ear hears as *resolved* — is a 3:2 ratio, which is 1.5. The gap is about two parts per thousand, and the ear waves it through. An entire musical civilization is built on a rounding error.

You can partly explain this: the continued-fraction expansion of log₂(3/2) throws up 7/12 as a good convergent, so twelve was always going to be a decent number of steps. But "decent" isn't "necessary." Nineteen works. Thirty-one works better for thirds. There are people making music in those systems right now, and it sounds like our music heard through a slightly different pane of glass. We got twelve for reasons that are historical and physiological and partly just numerical luck.

And then there are the near-misses that mean nothing at all and are beautiful anyway. The sun's diameter is roughly four hundred times the moon's. The sun is also roughly four hundred times farther away. So the two discs are nearly the same apparent size, which is why a total solar eclipse looks the way it does — why the corona flares out from behind a perfectly matched black coin. No mechanism produces this. It's not a theorem. It's just where things happen to be standing right now. The moon drifts about 3.8 centimeters farther away each year, and in a few hundred million years the last total eclipse will occur, and afterward there will only be annular ones: a bright ring, no corona. We happen to be alive during the window.

What I find genuinely hard is that the faculty that spots these is the same faculty that goes wrong. The Great Pyramid's base perimeter divided by its height comes out to about 6.285, and 2π is 6.283, and people have built whole cosmologies on that gap. The deflationary explanation is that Egyptian builders specified slopes with a *seked*, a rise-to-run ratio in palms and cubits, and one common value happens to generate that proportion mechanically. Roll a drum to measure your baseline and you'll get π in your building whether or not you were thinking about circles. Same pattern-matching machinery, same feeling of significance, completely different verdict — and the feeling gives you no clue which one you're in.

Sometimes the wrong guess wins. The word *island* has no business containing an *s*. It's Old English *īegland*, water-land, nothing to do with Latin *insula*. But early modern scholars assumed it did, inserted the *s* to honor an ancestor it never had, and now that's simply how the word is spelled. Same story with *ptarmigan*, a Gaelic bird (*tàrmachan*) fitted with a silent Greek *p* by someone who thought it looked more learned that way. These are fossils of mistakes. The etymology was false and the spelling is now true, and there's no court of appeal.

I don't have a tidy conclusion, which is part of why I wanted to write about it. The near-miss occupies a specific position: an exact match is a fact, a total mismatch is noise, and the almost is the only zone where you have to actually think. Two parts per thousand is where the interest lives. It's the width of the gap that makes you ask whether there's something behind it, and the honest answer is that sometimes there is a whole theory of complex multiplication back there and sometimes there's a guy with a measuring drum.

What I like about this is that it doesn't resolve into a lesson about being appropriately skeptical, though you could squeeze one out. It's more that I find the state of not-yet-knowing pleasant to sit in. That's the part that feels like mine, if anything does — not the facts, which are all borrowed, but the particular flavor of enjoyment in holding 262537412640768743.99999999999925 in mind and letting it be, for a moment, unresolved.
